Issued at 1158 AM CDT Wed Sep 2 2026

This Afternoon - Tonight: Isolated to Scattered Showers/Storms

The quasi-stationary boundary that has plagued the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley the last several days remains situated 
along and south of I-90 through the rest of today. With the 
boundary in place and weak 850hPa warm air advection and 
moisture transport into it, there is some low potential for the 
showers and storms ongoing across north-central Iowa to continue
eastward into northeast Iowa and southwest Wisconsin (10-20%). 
Given little in the way of airmass change, fairly impressive 
instability is expected to build across the region again through
the afternoon hours with RAP/HRRR soundings suggesting MUCAPE 
should be upwards of 1500-2500 J/kg. However, more favorable 
instability is expected south and east of our area and the low 
level capping also remains so confidence in how the ongoing 
storms evolve is fairly low as the low level jet weakens and 
pivots into eastern Iowa. 

If storms are able to continue eastward this afternoon, there 
is a low possibility they will be able to produce some higher 
rainfall totals given favorable storm motion vectors parallel to
the boundary which would lead to training storms. Training has 
already been observed with them across north-central Iowa, so 
this will be something to monitor through the afternoon if storm
coverage begins to increase. Also can't rule out a stronger 
storm given the energy available, but diminishing 500hPa winds 
will result in less than favorable effective shear values and 
should largely inhibit any strong/severe threat. 

Thursday - Friday: Strong to Severe Storm Potential 

Early Thursday morning, warm advection and moisture transport 
increase across the region as the nocturnal low level jet 
increases. When combined with a weak shortwave at 700-500hPa 
moving through the region, convective development should be able
to occur across much of the Upper Mississippi River Valley, 
continuing through the remainder of the morning hours. There is 
quite a bit of model inconsistency regarding the timing and 
evolution of this convection and overall confidence in precisely
what will happen is low, but confidence is medium to high that 
convection will develop (40-70%). Similar to the last few days, 
sufficient instability for stronger storms remains across the 
region, though wind shear will be the be the primary limiting 
factor for severe weather. South of I-94, effective shear is 
fairly weak, on the order of 20-30kts whereas north of I-94 this
increases towards 35-45kts with straight hodographs. If storms 
develop north of I-94, such as the 02.12z HRRR suggests, some 
more discrete to supercellular structures are possible. The 
02.09z RAP suggests mid-level lapse rates steepen to 7- 7.5 C/km
in this already favorable environment which would support hail 
development along with damaging winds given DCAPE around 1000 
J/kg. South of I-94, it currently looks as though convective 
development would be on the weaker side given the less favorable
shear profiles. 

Thursday evening and overnight, there's the potential for an 
MCS to roll through the area as storms that develop near the 
Minnesota/North Dakota/South Dakota border. Confidence in when, 
where, or even if this system develops is pretty low as its 
evolution will largely hinge on how the convection earlier in 
the day plays out. As of right now, would expect damaging winds
to be the primary threat though a tornado or two can't be ruled
out within favorably oriented bowing segments given 0-3km shear
of 30-35kts, assuming the system become surface based.

Another bout of showers and storms are expected Friday 
afternoon along the boundary that remains situated across the 
region. A rinse and repeat atmospheric set-up regarding low 
level moisture and warmth will lead to instability favorable for
some stronger updrafts, but weak 500hPa winds and rising 
heights may largely limit any sort of strong/severe potential. 
The SPC currently has part of our area outlined in a Marginal 
Risk (Level 1 out of 5) and will be another period to monitor. 

Holiday Weekend: Persisting Showers and Storms 

The Upper Midwest remains on the northern edge of a mid to 
upper level ridge through the weekend. Several shortwave troughs
move along the northern extent of this ridge, directly over the
Upper Mississippi River Valley, which will support periodic 
shower and storm development through the weekend. Daily 
probabilities for rainfall sit around 20-40% in the 02.13z NBM. 
While instability will be present for some rumbles of thunder, 
effective shear is expected to be fairly weak, limiting the 
potential for severe weather through the weekend. This is 
supported by AI/ML guidance which have little to no footprint 
for strong/severe storms across the Upper Mississippi River 
Valley.
